2: I have gathered everything I could learn about the story of poor Werther, and I set it before you here, certain that you will thank me for it.
You cannot refuse your admiration and your love to his spirit and his character, nor hold back your tears from his fate.
3: And you, good soul, who suffer the same distress he once endured — take comfort from his sorrows.
Let this little book be your friend, if fortune or your own fault has left you unable to find a dearer companion.
5: How happy I am to be gone!
My dear friend, what a strange thing the human heart is!
To leave you, whom I have never been apart from, whom I love so dearly — and still to feel happy!
I know you will forgive me.
Weren't my other attachments appointed by fate precisely to torment a mind like mine?
Poor Leonora! And yet I was not to blame.
Was it my fault that while her sister's peculiar charms were giving me pleasant entertainment, a passion for me took root in her frail heart?
And yet, am I entirely blameless?
Did I not encourage her feelings?
Didn't I delight in those genuine outpourings of nature that so often amused us, though there was really little in them to laugh at?
Didn't I — but oh, what is man, that he dares to accuse himself like this?
My dear friend, I promise you I will do better.
I will no longer brood over every petty vexation fortune deals out, as I have always done.
I will enjoy the present, and the past shall be past for me.
No doubt you are right, my best of friends: there would be far less suffering among people if they did not work their imaginations so hard at recalling old sorrows.
God knows why we are made this way, instead of simply bearing our present lot calmly.
Please tell my mother that I will handle her business as well as I can, and will send her word about it as soon as possible.
I have seen my aunt, and she is nothing like the disagreeable woman our friends make her out to be.
She is a lively, cheerful woman with the best of hearts.
I explained my mother's grievance about the part of her portion that has been withheld from her.
She told me her own motives and reasons, and the terms on which she is willing to give up the whole of it — and to do more than we asked.
In short, I cannot write any further about it now.
Only assure my mother that all will go well.
And once again, my dear friend, this trifling affair has shown me that misunderstanding and neglect cause more mischief in the world than malice and wickedness do.
At any rate, the last two are rarer.
6: In other ways I am very comfortable here.
Solitude in this earthly paradise is a balm to my mind.
The young spring, with all its generous promises, warms a heart that so often misgives me.
Every tree, every bush is in full flower.
You could wish yourself turned into a butterfly, to drift about in this ocean of scent and find your whole existence in it.
7: But all around it lies a beauty of nature beyond describing.
That is what moved the late Count M to lay out a garden on one of these sloping hills, which cross one another in the most charming variety and form the loveliest valleys.
The garden is a simple one.
From the moment you enter, you can tell it was not designed by a trained gardener, but by a man who wanted a place to give himself up to the feelings of his own heart.
I have already shed many a tear for its dead master in a summer-house that is now falling into ruin.
It was his favourite retreat, and now it is mine.
I shall soon be master of the place.
The gardener has grown fond of me these last few days, and he will be no worse off for it.
9: A wonderful serenity has taken possession of my whole soul, like these sweet spring mornings that I enjoy with all my heart.
I am alone, and I feel the charm of simply existing in this place, which was made for souls like mine.
I am so happy, my dear friend, so absorbed in the exquisite sense of quiet existence, that I neglect my art.
I could not draw a single stroke at this moment.
And yet I feel I have never been a greater artist than I am now.

When the lovely valley steams with mist around me, and the high sun rests on the surface of the impenetrable leaves of my trees, and only a few stray gleams steal into the inner sanctuary, I throw myself down in the tall grass by the trickling stream.
Lying close to the earth, I notice a thousand unfamiliar plants.

When I hear the hum of the little world among the stalks, and grow familiar with the countless indescribable forms of the insects and the flies, then I feel the presence of the Almighty, who made us in his own image.
I feel the breath of that universal love which bears and sustains us, floating around us in an eternity of bliss.
And then, my friend, when darkness comes over my eyes, and heaven and earth seem to rest in my soul and absorb its power, like the form of a beloved woman — then I often think with longing:
Oh, if only I could describe all this.
If only I could breathe onto paper everything that lives so full and warm within me, so that it might become the mirror of my soul, as my soul is the mirror of the infinite God.
Oh, my friend — but it is too much for my strength.
I sink under the weight and splendour of these visions.
11: I do not know whether some deceiving spirits haunt this place, or whether it is the warm, heavenly imagination in my own heart that makes everything around me seem like paradise.
In front of the house there is a fountain — a fountain I am bound to by a spell, like Melusina and her sisters.
You go down a gentle slope and come to an arch; some twenty steps further down, water of the clearest crystal gushes out of the marble rock.
The low wall that encloses it above, the tall trees that ring the spot, the coolness of the place itself — everything gives an impression at once pleasant and solemn.
Not a day passes that I do not spend an hour there.
The young girls come out from the town to fetch water — innocent, necessary work, and once the occupation of kings' daughters.
As I rest there, the old patriarchal life wakes up around me.
I see them, our ancestors, forming their friendships and making their alliances at the fountain-side.
And I feel how fountains and streams were watched over by kindly spirits.
Anyone who is a stranger to these feelings has never really known cool rest beside a fountain after a weary summer day.
13: You ask whether you should send me books.
My dear friend, for the love of God, I beg you — spare me that yoke!
I have no more need to be guided, stirred up, inflamed.
My heart ferments quite enough on its own.
What I want is music to lull me, and I find it perfectly in my Homer.
Often I struggle to calm the burning fever in my blood.
You have never seen anything so unsteady, so uncertain, as my heart.
But do I need to confess this to you, who have so often had to watch me swing from grief to wild joy, and from sweet melancholy to violent passion?
I treat my poor heart like a sick child and give in to its every whim.
Do not speak of this again — there are people who would blame me for it.
15: The ordinary people here know me already, and they are fond of me — the children especially.
When I first began to talk with them and ask in a friendly way about their small concerns, some thought I meant to make fun of them, and turned away from me in real ill humour.
I did not let it trouble me.
I only felt very keenly something I have often noticed before.
People of a certain rank keep coldly aloof from ordinary people, as though contact with them would cost them their standing.
Meanwhile idlers and bad jokers stoop to their level, only to make the poor feel their insolence all the more sharply.
16: I know perfectly well that we are not all equal, and cannot be.
But in my view, the man who keeps away from ordinary people in order not to lose their respect is as much to blame as a coward who hides from his enemy for fear of being beaten.
17: The other day I went down to the fountain and found a young servant-girl who had set her pitcher on the bottom step and was looking round to see whether one of her companions was coming to help her lift it onto her head.
I ran down and looked at her.
"Shall I help you, my girl?" I said.
She straightened the pad on her head, and I helped her.
She thanked me and went up the steps.
19: I have made all sorts of acquaintances, but so far I have found no real company.
I do not know what it is about me that attracts people; so many of them like me and attach themselves to me.
And then I am sorry when the road we travel together runs only a short way.
If you ask what the people here are like, I have to answer: the same as everywhere.
The human race is a monotonous business.
Most of them work the greater part of their lives merely to stay alive.
And the scrap of freedom left over troubles them so much that they will do anything to be rid of it.
20: But they are a thoroughly good sort of people.

Sometimes I forget myself and share in the innocent pleasures still left to country people — enjoying myself freely and sincerely round a well-filled table, arranging an outing or a dance at the right moment, and so on.
All of it does my spirits good.
Only I must not remember how many other powers lie sleeping in me, rotting unused, that I am obliged to keep carefully hidden.
Ah, that thought weighs on me terribly.
And yet to be misunderstood is the fate of people like us.
21: Oh, that the friend of my youth is gone!
Oh, that I ever knew her!
I might tell myself: "You are a dreamer, to look for what is not to be found here on earth."
I possessed that heart, that noble soul, in whose presence I seemed more than I really was, because I was everything I was capable of being.
Good heavens! Was a single power of my soul left unused?
In her presence, could I not unfold to the full that mysterious feeling with which my heart takes hold of nature?
Wasn't everything between us a constant weaving of the finest feeling and the keenest wit, whose every variation — even at its most eccentric — bore the stamp of genius?
And the few years by which she was older than me brought her to the grave before me.
I can never forget her steady mind or her heavenly patience.
22: A few days ago I met a young man called V—, frank and open, with a most pleasing face.
He has just left the university.
He does not think himself a great sage, but he does believe he knows more than other people.
He has worked hard — I can tell that from a dozen things — and in short he has a large stock of information.

When he heard that I draw a good deal and that I know Greek — two remarkable things in this part of the country — he came to see me and unpacked his whole store of learning, from Batteaux to Wood, from De Piles to Winkelmann.
He assured me he had read right through the first part of Sultzer's theory, and that he owned a manuscript of Heyne's work on the study of antiquity.
I let it all go by.
23: I have also got to know a very worthy man, the district judge — frank and open-hearted.
They tell me it is a delightful sight to see him among his children; he has nine of them.
His eldest daughter especially is spoken of very highly.
He has invited me to visit, and I mean to go at the first opportunity.
He lives at one of the royal hunting-lodges, an hour and a half away on foot.
He was given leave to live there after losing his wife, since it is so painful for him to stay in town and at the court.
24: A few other odd characters have crossed my path as well — questionable sorts, undesirable in every way, and most unbearable in their displays of friendship.
This letter will please you — it is quite historical.
